title: HTTP Digest Access Authentication
summary: Defines HTTP Digest Access Authentication, a challenge-response scheme in which the client proves it knows a password without sending it in the clear. It updates earlier Digest specifications and supports stronger hash algorithms.

eli5.summary: Instead of saying the secret word, you show a scrambled version made from it plus a number the server gave you.

questions: what does the cnonce parameter do
subtitle: A challenge-response login for HTTP that proves you know a password without sending it, now with SHA-256.

tldr.problem: HTTP needs a way for a client to prove it knows a password without sending the password in the clear, as Basic authentication does.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a one-time nonce in a 401 challenge. The client replies with a digest computed from the username, realm, password, nonce, request method and URI, plus its own client nonce.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7616 adds SHA-256 and SHA-512/256, username hashing and internationalization rules. The RFC calls Digest weak by modern cryptographic standards but far better than Basic.

today: RFC 7616 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2617. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is the current definition of Digest authentication.

sections.title: What Digest Authentication Is
sections.content:
HTTP has a simple challenge-response framework in which a server challenges a client request and the client supplies authentication information. RFC 7616 defines the Digest scheme for that framework. The framework itself is specified in RFC 7235.

The scheme extends, and is generally backward compatible with, RFC 2617. The RFC states that this document, together with the Basic scheme definition in RFC 7617, the Authentication-Info definitions in RFC 7615 and RFC 7235, obsoletes RFC 2617.

The overall idea is simple. The server challenges using a nonce value. A valid response contains an unkeyed digest of the username, the password, the nonce, the HTTP method and the requested URI. The password is never sent in the clear. The username and password must be prearranged in a way this document does not address.
sections.eli5: It is a secret handshake where you never say the password out loud. You mix it with a number the server picked and show only the mixed-up result.

sections.title: The Challenge and the Reply
sections.content:
When a request for a protected object arrives without an acceptable Authorization header field, the server answers 401 Unauthorized with a WWW-Authenticate header field using the Digest scheme. Its parameters include:

  • realm: a string shown to users, which should contain at least the host name.
  • domain: URIs that define the protection space.
  • nonce: a server-specified string that should be uniquely generated each time a 401 is made. It is opaque to the client.
  • opaque: data the client SHOULD return unchanged in later requests in the same protection space.
  • stale: tells the client the nonce was out of date, so it can retry without asking the user again.
  • algorithm, qop, charset and userhash, covered in the next sections.

The client retries with an Authorization header carrying username, realm, uri, response, a client nonce cnonce and a nonce count nc. The nc value is the hexadecimal count of requests sent with that nonce, such as nc=00000001, and exactly 8 hexadecimal digits. The uri repeats the request target because proxies can change it in transit.

The server may then confirm success in an Authentication-Info header, optionally giving a nextnonce for one-time nonces, and an rspauth digest that lets the client check the server knows the secret too. Proxies use the same scheme with status 407 and the Proxy-Authenticate and Proxy-Authorization header fields. Proxies MUST forward the ordinary Digest header fields untouched.
sections.eli5: The server hands you a random number, and you answer with a scrambled code made from the number, your password and what you are asking for. You also add your own random number so nobody can trick you.

sections.title: Computing the Response
sections.content:
The response is a hex string. With qop set to auth or auth-int it is KD(H(A1), nonce:nc:cnonce:qop:H(A2)). H is the chosen hash and KD(secret, data) is H of the secret, a colon and the data.

A1 covers the credentials: username:realm:password. For a -sess algorithm variant, such as SHA-256-sess, A1 instead hashes those three values and then appends the server nonce and the client nonce. That makes a fresh session key for each authentication session and allows third-party authentication servers that hold only the hash of the credentials.

A2 covers the request: Method:request-uri for qop=auth. With qop=auth-int it also adds H(entity-body), which gives limited integrity protection.

The digest is written as hexadecimal characters, 32 for MD5 and 64 for SHA-256 and SHA-512/256. No white space is allowed in the strings being hashed unless it is part of a quoted value, so a password with spaces keeps them.
sections.eli5: You stir the password, the server's number and what you are asking for into a pot, then show only the soup. Nobody can un-stir it to get the password back.

sections.title: Algorithms and Negotiation
sections.content:
This RFC adds two algorithms to the one in RFC 2617. SHA2-256 is mandatory to implement, SHA2-512/256 is a backup, and MD5 remains only for backward compatibility and is NOT RECOMMENDED. If no algorithm parameter is present, MD5 is assumed.

A server can offer several choices by sending several WWW-Authenticate header fields. Each challenge MUST use a different digest algorithm, and the server MUST list them from most preferred to least preferred. The client SHOULD use the first challenge it supports, unless local policy says otherwise. If it does not understand an algorithm, it should ignore that challenge.

New hash algorithms go in a new IANA registry, Hash Algorithms for HTTP Digest Authentication, with update policy Specification Required. It starts with MD5, SHA-512-256 and SHA-256.
sections.eli5: The server lists the scramblers it knows, best first, and you pick the first one you also know. The old scrambler is still there, but only for old friends.

sections.title: Username Hashing and Character Encoding
sections.content:
To protect the username in transit, a server SHOULD set userhash=true in its challenge. A client that supports it MUST then send the hash H(username:realm), using the same algorithm, and include userhash=true in its Authorization header.

For international text, servers SHOULD send charset in the challenge. The only allowed value is UTF-8, which means usernames and passwords are converted to Unicode Normalization Form C and encoded as UTF-8 before hashing. When a username cannot be sent hashed and contains non-ASCII characters, the client can use the username* parameter instead. Sending both username and username* MUST be treated as an error.
sections.eli5: Even your name can be scrambled so a snoop cannot see who is logging in. And everyone agrees on one way to write letters from all languages so the scramble comes out the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is frank about the limits. By modern cryptographic standards, Digest Authentication is weak. With human-memorable passwords it is vulnerable to dictionary attacks, which are much easier than attacks on the hash algorithms themselves, so algorithm agility does not help. It SHOULD be used only with passwords of reasonable entropy, for example 128 bits or more, and SHOULD be used over a secure channel like HTTPS.

It offers no confidentiality beyond protecting the username and password, only limited integrity protection, and no way for the client to authenticate the server unless rspauth is checked. The server's password file holds username and H(A1) values, and must be protected as if it contained plain passwords. Putting the realm in the digest means one compromised file does not directly compromise others with the same username and password.

A man-in-the-middle can offer only Basic authentication, or add a weak scheme. A client SHOULD always use the strongest scheme it understands.

The client nonce cnonce is the countermeasure against chosen plaintext, precomputed dictionary and batch brute-force attacks. Replay is addressed by server nonce design, such as timestamps, one-time nonces or qop=auth-int for POST and PUT. The RFC concludes that any compliant implementation is relatively weak by cryptographic standards, but far superior to Basic Authentication.
sections.eli5: This lock is better than a flimsy one but it is not a vault. Easy-to-guess passwords can still be cracked, so use long random ones and a secure connection too.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2617
sections.content:
Appendix A lists what is new compared with RFC 2617:

  • SHA2-256 is mandatory and SHA2-512/256 is a backup, with algorithm negotiation defined. MD5 is kept only for backward compatibility.
  • Username hashing, mainly for privacy reasons.
  • Internationalization considerations that affect the A1 calculation and username and password encoding.
  • A new IANA registry for hash algorithms.
  • Backward compatibility with RFC 2069 is deprecated.
sections.eli5: It is an upgraded version with a stronger scrambler, hidden names, support for all languages and a retired old mode.

messages.label: 401 Unauthorized + WWW-Authenticate: Digest
messages.note: Carries realm, nonce, qop, algorithm and opaque.

messages.label: GET with Authorization: Digest
messages.note: Carries username, response, cnonce and nc.

data.title: Digest response with qop=auth
data.code:
A1 = unq(username) ":" unq(realm) ":" passwd
A2 = Method ":" request-uri

response = KD ( H(A1), unq(nonce)
                       ":" nc
                       ":" unq(cnonce)
                       ":" unq(qop)
                       ":" H(A2) )
